finding: Item 1's assertion is unreachable for `tp import`. import does not merge: it writes the document it was handed via WriteTaskFile, and its existence guard refuses when the target already holds tasks (`task file already exists: <path> (use --force to overwrite)`, exit 3) unless `--force`. Serializing it behind the lock does not change that. Under the lock the two orderings give different results: import first, then the other writer's `add` appends → both tasks present; the other writer first, then import → import re-reads a non-empty target and exits 3. "The test holds the write lock, starts `tp import`, releases, and asserts the final file contains both writers' tasks" describes the second ordering and asserts the first ordering's outcome.

resolved.evidence: Test item 1 no longer asserts a merge import does not perform. It asserts the lock property: a writer starting while the lock is held reads only post-release content.

suggestion: Name the two writers and the ordering. Either make the lock holder the importer and the blocked writer `tp add` (then "both writers' tasks" holds), or keep import blocked and assert the correct serialized outcome — exit 3 from the existence guard, with the first writer's task intact and byte-identical — which is the behaviour the fix actually buys.

finding: Item 1's recipe (hold the write lock, start `tp import`, release, assert the final file contains both writers' tasks) never says when the lock-holder writes its own task relative to import's read, and names no rendezvous proving import actually reached the lock before the release. Both omissions decide whether the test can fail against today's unlocked import: if the holder's write lands before import reads, or if the release happens before import even starts, an unlocked import also produces a file containing both tasks and the test passes green over the defect. Determinism without a pinned interleaving buys reproducibility at the cost of discrimination - two engineers write tests with opposite failure behaviour on the unfixed tree.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 0. The rendezvous is now explicit — take lock, rewrite target, start import, release — and the test fails against today's unlocked read.

suggestion: State the interleaving as an ordered sequence with an explicit synchronization point: holder acquires the lock; import is started and observed blocked on acquisition (signal file, test seam, or polling the lock); only then the holder writes task A and releases; import must read post-A state and write A+B. Add the negative acceptance the test must satisfy: with the lock acquisition removed from the import path the test fails on every run.

finding: Item 11's equality has no readable right-hand side. §7.1 says the release's first task "produces the list as its only output" without naming a path or a record format, and "the surviving subset" is the outcome of per-test sweep decisions recorded only in closing evidence, which §2 states nothing parses. §8.2 and §8.3 each give their equality a stated source on both sides; item 11 gives one side only, so it cannot be written as a test. The set boundary is also open: §7.1 caps the sweep at "that list plus any test a removal decision depends on", so a marked guard from that second group would break an equality defined over the list alone.

resolved.evidence: Test item 11 and the // guard: marker are deleted. The list has a named home, spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md, and is the sweep's cap rather than one side of an equality.

suggestion: Require the first task to write a committed artifact (name the path and the record shape, e.g. {file, function, defect, disposition}), require removals and rewrites to update it in the same task, and restate item 11 as: the set of `// guard:` markers found in the tree equals the set of records with disposition `kept`. State explicitly whether tests pulled in by a removal decision may carry the marker.

finding: The repaired item 11 asserts that the set of tests carrying a '// guard:' marker equals the surviving subset of §7.1's list 'and no unlisted test carries the marker', while §7.1 freezes that list to guards added during the v0.31.2, v0.32.0 and v0.33.0 audits and in the same breath establishes the marker as the convention that 'makes the class mechanically enumerable from then on'. The two clauses are incompatible going forward: the next audit-added guard that follows the convention is by construction unlisted, so it fails item 11 — and the next audit is v0.35.0's unattended run, where a red gate on correct behaviour is the expensive failure this release exists to prevent.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 2: the frozen-set oracle is gone with the marker.

suggestion: Make the equality one-directional or time-bounded: every test on §7.1's surviving list carries the marker (a subset check), or pin the closed equality to this release's own commit and state that later guards extend the marker set freely.

finding: §12 item 11 requires that the set of tests carrying a `// guard:` marker equals the surviving subset of §7.1's list and that 'no unlisted test carries the marker', while §7.1 says the marker is what 'makes the class mechanically enumerable from then on'. §7.1's list is derived from the v0.31.2/v0.32.0/v0.33.0 commits, so no test written in this release can be on it — yet this release adds guards of exactly that kind (§12 items 1-8 and §5's config-assertion guard). Either those new guards carry the marker and item 11's test goes red (a gate failure every later close in the release inherits), or they are left unmarked and the enumeration is already incomplete on the day it ships.
suggestion: Restate item 11 as a one-time sweep assertion over §7.1's list only (every listed test that survives carries a marker; no listed test that was removed or rewritten still does; no test that predates the sweep and is off the list carries one), and state in §7.1 that guards added by this and later releases carry the marker as they are written.

finding: The §2 repair (round 1 idx 4) removed the additive escape hatch ('a task that only adds is not forbidden, but it is the exception') and replaced it with a closed binary: every task is a removal task or a repair task on 'one of the defects in §1 and §9', and 'A task that is neither does not belong in this release.' Most of this release's own work is neither kind: §7.1's first task produces a list and removes nothing, §5's config guard test, §8.2's and §8.3's equality tests, §12 items 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11, and the pure documentation additions of §10.1 and §10.2. Round 1's finding already named that set as the reason the old rule was toothless; the repair made the rule binding without giving those tasks a legal kind, so §2 now forbids the tasks §5, §7, §8, §10 and §12 mandate.

resolved.evidence: Section 2 no longer closes the taxonomy. A task that only adds belongs here when a section of the spec mandates the addition and its acceptance cites that section.

suggestion: Add a third declared kind — an 'instrument' task (a check, marker, test or document that makes a later removal verifiable) — legitimate only when a named section of this spec requires it; or scope the binary explicitly to the code and documentation sweeps of §6-§8.

finding: §2 binds decomposition to exactly two kinds of task — a removal (naming what it removes and what still covers it) or a repair ("one of the defects in §1 and §9") — and states "a task that is neither does not belong in this release". At least five tasks the spec itself mandates are neither: §7.1's first task (produces the guard list, pure addition), §8.2's exported lint-rule enumeration plus its equality test, §8.3's new flag inventory in SKILL.md plus its equality test, and §10.1/§10.2's two documentation additions. None removes anything and none repairs a §1 or §9 defect, so the operator applying the governing rule at task-list review has to either reject them or silently break the rule on the first pass.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 5: the release's own list task, guard test, equality tests and doc additions are all mandated by cited sections.

suggestion: Add a third declared kind — an 'enabling' or 'instrument' task, defined as work whose only output is the artifact a §7/§8 equality test or removal decision depends on — and name §7.1's list, §8.2's enumeration, §8.3's inventory and §10's documentation as its full membership, so the kind is closed rather than an escape hatch.

finding: §2 now closes the taxonomy: every task is either a removal task or a repair task ('one of the defects in §1 and §9'), and 'a task that is neither does not belong in this release.' Several work items this same spec mandates are neither: §7.1's first task, whose only output is the guard-test list; §8.2's exported enumeration of lint rule identifiers and its equality test; §8.3's added flag documentation and its equality test; §5's config-assertion guard test; and §7.1's `// guard:` comments. A decomposer applying §2 literally must reject the tasks §5, §7 and §8 require, so the governing rule and the release contents contradict each other.
suggestion: Either admit a third kind — a mechanization task, whose output is a check/enumeration/equality test that stops a stated fact from drifting — or restate §2's fence as 'a task implements only what a named section of this spec requires; nothing is added that no section asks for', which keeps the anti-drift intent without excluding §5/§7/§8.

finding: The premise is false against the tree. §5 says "`tp init` writes a `quality_gate` into each `<base>.tasks.json`" and "every one of this repo's task files currently masks the project gate with a copy that has no `-race`". init.go only sets Workflow.QualityGate when `--quality-gate` was passed (it is `initQualityGate != ""`-guarded), and of the 23 `spec/*.tasks.json` files exactly two carry a task-level `quality_gate`: `spec/0.31.0.tasks.json` and `spec/0.34.0.tasks.json`. The other 21 hold no override and already resolve to the project default, so the stated repair ("removing the redundant overrides") is a two-file edit, not the sweep §5 describes — and one of the two is this release's own task file, the other a shipped historical record whose stored gate is part of what it recorded.

resolved.evidence: The false premise is deleted. Measured: two task files carry the override, 0.31.0 and 0.34.0, and tp init writes it only when --quality-gate is passed.

suggestion: Restate the premise on the measured facts: two task files carry the override, name them, and say whether the historical `spec/0.31.0.tasks.json` override is removed (rewriting a closed release's record) or left and exempted. Then say what §12 item 5's guard does with an exempted file, since it asserts on every `spec/*.tasks.json`.

finding: The §5 repair (round 1 idx 7) fixes the instances but not the generator. The same paragraph states that 'tp init writes a quality_gate into each <base>.tasks.json, and a task-level value wins over the project default', then requires only that the redundant overrides in today's files be removed. Nothing changes what tp init writes, so the next init-authored task file re-masks the project gate — and the next one is v0.35.0's, the unattended run §1 says this release is scheduled to protect. The §12 item 5 guard is asserted over 'every spec/*.tasks.json', so the first legitimately created v0.35.0 task file makes that guard fail: the check fires on a new file rather than catching the regression. Round 1's finding named the v0.35.0 init-authored file specifically; the repair addressed only the files that exist today.

resolved.evidence: The generator is addressed in the same paragraph: later releases omit --quality-gate at init, and the guard fails on a reintroduced override as well as on a weakened project gate.

suggestion: State what happens at the next init: either this release's decomposition mandates --quality-gate with -race for v0.35.0 and §5 says so, or init stops writing a task-level quality_gate when the project layer already resolves one, or §12 item 5 is scoped to task files that carry an override so a fresh file is not a false failure.

finding: Round 1 idx 29 warned that a unit satisfies §6.1 completely by choosing a threshold high enough that dupl reports nothing. The repair pins a starting value but writes that escape into the spec: 'the threshold is raised instead — to the lowest value at which the tree is clean'. A clean tree is a report with no clones, so a single clone that would need a new abstraction (Non-Goal 7) licenses raising a global knob until every other clone — including the mergeable ones — leaves the report too, and the task's stated acceptance ('golangci-lint run is clean with dupl enabled') is then met having removed nothing. The per-site exemption the same paragraph already offers ('exempted with a reason at the site') is the local instrument for a local exemption, and no ordering requires merges to be attempted before the raise.

resolved.evidence: The threshold-raising escape is deleted. dupl runs at its default threshold, which is not raised.

suggestion: Order the three moves: merge what merges, exempt the Non-Goal 7 clones individually at the site with a reason, and raise the threshold only when per-site exemption is impossible. If the raise stays, bound what it may hide — raised only past the single clone that forced it, with the exempted clones listed in the task's evidence.

finding: §6.1 never says whether `dupl` runs over `_test.go`, and that decision is the whole size of the task. Measured on this tree with golangci-lint v2.12.2 at dupl's default threshold: 13 issues, of which 11 are in test files (audit_record_advisory_test.go≡review_record_advisory_test.go, two pairs inside review_test.go, brief_prior_test.go, configresolve_test.go) and exactly one production clone pair exists (internal/cli/review.go:1471-1506 ≡ 1508-1543). So the acceptance "`golangci-lint run` is clean with `dupl` enabled" is overwhelmingly a test refactor, which collides with §7.4 (tests the sweep must not touch) and with Non-Goal 7 (extracting a shared test helper to merge two table-driven tests is designing a new abstraction). §6.1's motivating examples are all production code, so the requirement as written does not build what it argues for.

resolved.evidence: Section 6.1 states that dupl covers production and test files alike, and records the measurement: 13 issues, 11 in _test.go, one production clone pair named by file and line range.

suggestion: State the scope: either set `run.tests: false` (or a `_test.go` exclusion) so `dupl` covers production code only — and say so in the acceptance — or keep tests in scope and pre-declare that test clones are exempted at the site with a reason rather than merged, so the task cannot be read as a licence to refactor guarded tests.

finding: "The guard tests added during the v0.31.2, v0.32.0 and v0.33.0 audit rounds, named `file:function`, derived from those releases' commits" still needs two judgements the spec does not pin. First, which commits are audit-round commits: the history distinguishes task closes from audit repairs only by convention, and no marker, trailer, path or subject pattern is named. Second, which tests added in that window are guards rather than feature or coverage tests - §7.1 itself rules authorial intent unobservable, and those releases added substantial feature test surface. Nothing states how a test renamed, moved or split since is resolved. Two engineers therefore produce materially different lists, and both the sweep scope and item 11's equality inherit the difference.

resolved.evidence: The derivation is now mechanical: every test function added or modified by a commit falling between the record-audit-round commits of the three releases.

suggestion: Give a mechanical derivation (e.g. test functions added by commits between two tags whose subject matches a named prefix, or that touched `.tp-review/`), or drop derivation and make the artifact authoritative: the first task enumerates candidates from a stated commit range and the operator-approved file becomes the source of truth. Either way, state the rule for entries whose test has since been renamed or removed.

finding: Round 1 idx 3 and idx 32 rejected item 11 because the record it rested on named 'no artifact, no location and no format'. The repair moved that dependency rather than removing it: item 11's equality now needs §7.1's list — specifically 'the surviving subset' of it — as a machine-readable input, and §7.1 says only that the release's first task 'produces the list as its only output', with no path, no format, and no place where the keep/rewrite/remove decision per entry is recorded. The marker side is greppable; the other side of the equality is still prose, so the item is unrunnable for the same reason it was rewritten. This class has now taken three prose corrections, which is where CLAUDE.md says to write the check instead.

resolved.evidence: The dependency is removed rather than relocated: no equality remains, and the list itself has a path.

suggestion: Name the artifact and its format in §7.1 — a committed file of 'file:function' lines with a per-entry disposition (kept | rewritten | removed, with the surviving coverage named) — and have item 11 read it. That file is also the enumeration §2.1's middle row needs.

finding: The list has no stated home. §7.1 makes the release's first task produce the `file:function` guard list "as its only output", and §12 item 11 asserts an equality between the set of tests carrying `// guard:` and "the surviving subset of §7.1's list" — a Go test cannot compare against a list that exists nowhere on disk. Closing evidence is explicitly ruled out as a source by §2 ("Nothing in tp parses closing evidence and this release adds nothing that will"), and a `closed_reason` string in `spec/0.34.0.tasks.json` is not a format any test can read. The implementer of the first task cannot tell what to write, and the implementer of item 11 cannot tell what to read.

resolved.evidence: The list's home is spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md, one file:function per line.

suggestion: Name the artifact and its format — e.g. a committed `spec/0.34.0-guards.txt`, one `file:function` per line, ordered — say who removes a line when a guard is removed under §7.1's last paragraph, and restate item 11 as an equality between that file and the `// guard:`-marked set.

finding: Item 9 asserts "the documented lint rule set equals the engine's emitted rule set", but §8.2's mechanism only checks the table against "an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers". Nothing binds that enumeration to what the engine actually emits, so a rule emitted from a site that never registers in the enumeration satisfies the enumeration and the table while the documentation stays incomplete - the exact drift the section exists to prevent, moved one hop down. The section also states no failure mode: what fails, with what message, when a new rule is added.

resolved.evidence: Test 9 gained a second assertion binding the enumeration to what the engine emits, so the documented set cannot pass while the enumeration is incomplete.

suggestion: Make the enumeration the only source of emitted identifiers (every emitted rule id constructed from the enumerated constants, so an unregistered rule cannot be emitted), or add a second check deriving the emitted set from the emission sites. Then state both failure modes: adding an identifier to the enumeration without a table row fails the table test; emitting an identifier absent from the enumeration fails the source test.

finding: `tp init` has no missing-spec code path at all, so it cannot "currently emit the code-3 task-file default hint on a missing file". runInit never stats the spec: it derives the task-file path from the argument, stats the TASK file, and writes. Its exit-3 sites are task-file-already-exists, the task-file write error, the `.tp` MkdirAll and EnsureTPGitignore — for the first of those the code-3 task-file default is the correct advice. `tp init missing.md` today exits 0 and creates `missing.tasks.json` (and `tp add --spec missing.md` reaches the same path). §12 item 8 therefore does not adopt a hint; it requires a new spec-existence check and a new failure where the command previously succeeded, which Non-Goal 1's five enumerated behaviour changes do not cover.

resolved.evidence: Section 9.3 drops tp init and states why: runInit never stats the spec, so giving it a missing-spec path would be a new behaviour that Non-Goal 1 excludes.

suggestion: Split §9.3: for `lint`, an existing exit-3 site changes hint text; for `init`, state the new requirement explicitly — init stats the spec before deriving the task-file path and exits 3 with specFileMissingHint when it is absent — add it to Non-Goal 1's enumeration, and say which of init's other exit-3 sites keep the task-file default (so leaving `taskFileCommands` does not silently demand a hint at the MkdirAll/gitignore sites).

finding: §3 was widened to two unlocked write paths (`importcmd.go`, and `init.go` reached also by `tp add --spec`), but the headline artifacts still describe one: §1's defect table has a single row naming only '`tp import` writes the task file outside the write lock', §3's heading is still '`tp import` writes under the lock', and §11 refers to the §1 set as 'the three write defects'. §1's table is what §11 and any decomposition read as the release's defect inventory, so the second write path is invisible to every consumer of that inventory.
suggestion: Split the §1 row into two (import; init / `add --spec`) or reword it to 'task-file writes that run outside the write lock', widen §3's heading to match its body, and update §11's reference accordingly.

finding: §10.1 declares an `input → expected output` example table "the acceptance shape for behavioural tasks" and argues the source of the expected value is the only defence against tautological tests - yet this release's own behavioural changes ship without one: §4 gives no example of the over-cap abort line, §9.1 no command line paired with its exit code, and §9.2/§9.3 no before/after hint strings. Those are exactly the values a unit would otherwise obtain by running the code it just wrote, which §10.1 says is the failure to avoid.
suggestion: Add one example table per behavioural change (input command line → exit code → stderr hint), covering §9.2 and §9.3's hint text, §9.1's unknown-command case, and §4's over-cap abort line; the same table settles the abort message's wording that §4 leaves to the implementer.

finding: Non-Goal 1 claims the release "changes observable behaviour in exactly five places" and then names seven: the three §1 defects, the §9.1 exit code, the §9.2 hint, the §9.3 hint, and "plus the gate command in §5" — which double-counts, since the third §1 defect IS the missing -race gate. Under any reading the enumeration is six distinct behaviour changes, not five (and the -race defect is not a "write defect"). This list is the fence an auditor checks every diff against, so a count that does not match its own enumeration either invites a spurious FAIL or licenses a seventh change nobody notices; a wrong fence costs audit rounds, which is the most expensive round-trip in the whole workflow.
suggestion: State the list without a leading count, or fix it to the actual distinct set: "in exactly six places: the write-lock fix (§3), the bulk cap (§4), the gate command (§5), the exit code (§9.1), and the hints in §9.2 and §9.3". Drop "the three write defects of §1" as a group label since one of the three is the gate and none of the three is a write defect in the same sense.

finding: Non-Goal 1 says observable behaviour changes in "exactly five places" and then lists "the three write defects of §1, the exit code in §9.1, and the hint text in §9.2 and §9.3, plus the gate command in §5" - seven enumerated items, or six once the reader notices §1's third row and §5's gate are the same change. Five is reachable only by silently deduping the gate against §1 and merging the two hint changes into one. The sentence is meant to be the auditable fence around the three sweeps, so a reviewer must be able to check both membership and count; as written neither is checkable.
suggestion: Drop the number and give the fence as one line per change (import lock; bulk over-cap abort; gate `-race`; unknown-command exit 2; §9.2 hint; §9.3 hint), so "is this change inside the fence?" has exactly one answer.

finding: Non-Goal 1's enumeration does not reconcile with its own count or with §1. It claims 'exactly five places' and then lists: 'the three write defects of §1' (3) + the exit code in §9.1 (1) + the hint text in §9.2 and §9.3 (2) + 'plus the gate command in §5' (1) = seven. Worse, §1 itself describes two write paths plus 'a third defect' that is the gate, so calling all three 'write defects' and then adding the gate counts the gate twice — and §3's second write path (init.go, reached by `tp add --spec`) is not visible in the count at all.
suggestion: Enumerate the behaviour changes one clause per change and make the number match, e.g. six: the import lock, the init/`add --spec` lock, the bulk cap abort, the §9.1 exit code, the §9.2+§9.3 hint text, and the §5 gate command.

finding: Non-Goal 1's enumeration double-counts and does not sum to its own number. §1's table holds two write defects (import outside the lock, the bulk 64KB cap) and one gate defect (no `-race`); Non-Goal 1 calls all three "the three write defects of §1" and then adds "plus the gate command in §5", counting the gate twice, while claiming "exactly five places". Read as written the enumeration yields seven. This matters operationally because Non-Goal 1 is the fence a task uses to decide whether a change is in scope, and §7/§8 tasks are required to be behaviour-neutral against it.
suggestion: Correct to "the two write defects of §1" and keep "plus the gate command in §5", which makes the list sum to five: import locking, the bulk cap, the §9.1 exit code, the §9.2/§9.3 hint text, and the gate. Then add §9.3's new init failure once that is settled (see the §9.3 finding), and update the count.

finding: Non-Goal 3 says 'No new commands or flags. Every change is a fix, a removal, a hint, a test or a document.' §8.2 requires the engine to gain 'an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers' — new exported production API, which is none of the five permitted kinds — and §2.3 makes 'exported symbols' one of the five before-and-after counts the release records, so the release's own subtraction ledger moves the wrong way on a change its Non-Goals do not license.
suggestion: Name §8.2's enumeration as the release's one sanctioned addition and say why (it is the source of truth a check reads, i.e. it removes a class of drift), extend the permitted-kinds list to cover it, and state how it is accounted for in §2.3's exported-symbol delta.

finding: The Non-Goal 1 repair (idx 0/15) replaced an unenumerated claim with an enumeration that does not add up. It claims 'exactly five places' and then lists 'the three write defects of §1, the exit code in §9.1, and the hint text in §9.2 and §9.3, plus the gate command in §5' — six items, and §1's third row is the gate defect itself, so §5 is counted twice while only two of §1's rows are write defects at all. §3's new lock-timeout failure output for tp import and tp init is a further observable change that appears nowhere in the list. Non-Goal 1 is the fence a unit reads to decide whether a behaviour change is in scope, so a fence whose own count is wrong is the defect idx 0 was raised about, one revision on.
suggestion: Drop the count or make it match: enumerate as a list — (1) import/init locking including its exit-4 timeout path, (2) the bulk cap exit 3, (3) the gate command, (4) §9.1's exit code, (5) §9.2 and §9.3's hints — and stop calling §1's gate row a write defect.

finding: Item 11 asserts that the set of tests carrying a `// guard:` marker equals the surviving subset of §7.1's list "and no unlisted test carries the marker". §7.1 introduces the marker precisely so the guard class is "mechanically enumerable from then on" — but a closed-set equality against a frozen historical list (v0.31.2/v0.32.0/v0.33.0 guards) makes the marker unusable from then on: the first guard test written in v0.35.0 either goes unmarked, defeating the enumeration, or carries the marker and turns the gate red until someone edits a list from a shipped release. Every future audit round then pays an edit to a v0.34.0 artifact — a recurring tax on the unattended run this release is explicitly clearing the way for.
suggestion: Assert the one-way direction only: every test on §7.1's surviving list carries a `// guard:` marker (no unlisted-test clause), so new guards can join the class freely. If a closed set is wanted, scope the equality to the v0.34.0 sweep explicitly ("no test on the list lost its marker") and say in §7.1 that the marker set is open for later releases.

finding: Item 2 asserts exit 4 "with `LockTimeoutError`'s hint", and §3 says that hint names "the lock path and the elapsed wait". The elapsed wait is not reproducible, so string equality on the hint is flaky while a bare substring check may assert almost nothing, and the item does not say which is required. It also does not state how the timeout is forced - which `lock_timeout_seconds` value is configured - and with a documented floor of 1 second that choice sets the test's own runtime.
suggestion: State the assertion shape: the hint must contain the absolute lock path and a duration token (e.g. matching a 'waited <number>s' pattern), and name the `lock_timeout_seconds` value the test configures to force the timeout.

finding: §5 deliberately states the requirement on the resolved value as "the gate resolved for every spec/*.tasks.json in this repository contains `-race`", while §12 item 5 asserts the resolved gate "equals `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`". Contains and equals are different tests with different lifetimes: the equality pins the full gate string in a test, so any later gate change unrelated to this defect (an added flag, a script, a -timeout) fails a guard named for -race and costs a debugging round-trip to discover it is not about races at all. A task author also cannot tell which of the two the acceptance is.
suggestion: Pick one and use it in both places. Prefer the §5 wording — assert that every resolved gate contains `-race` — which is the property this release is defending and the one that survives future gate edits; if the exact-string equality is wanted, restate §5 as equality and say why pinning the whole command is intended.

finding: §5 states the requirement as "the gate resolved for every `spec/*.tasks.json` in this repository contains `-race`", while item 5 asserts the resolved gate equals `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`. Containment and equality are different guards: a task file whose gate legitimately adds a step passes §5 and fails item 5, and a future file that keeps an override containing `-race` passes §5 while defeating the subtraction §5 asks for. Two engineers write different config guards from the same release.
suggestion: Pick one strength and state it in both places. Equality matches §5's "reached by removing the redundant overrides" intent - if so, reword §5's bold sentence to "resolves to exactly `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`".

finding: §5 states the requirement as 'the gate resolved for every `spec/*.tasks.json` in this repository contains `-race`', while §12 item 5 asserts that the resolved gate 'equals `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`'. Equality is strictly stronger than containment: a task file resolving to any other gate that includes `-race` satisfies §5 and fails item 5, and equality additionally pins the exact command string, so any future legitimate per-spec gate breaks the test rather than the requirement.
suggestion: Choose one predicate and state it in both places. If equality is intended (it is the stronger guard against a masking override), make §5 say 'resolves to exactly `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`' and say what a spec that legitimately needs a different gate does.

finding: §2's binary - every task is a removal or one of the repairs of §1 and §9, and "a task that is neither does not belong in this release" - is a pass/fail check applied to the task list, and this release's own required work fails it. §8.2's exported enumeration and its equality test, §8.3's newly documented flags, §10.1 and §10.2's new SKILL.md sections, §7.1's `// guard:` comments and §12's new tests are additions, and none is a §1 or §9 defect. The reviewer applying §2 must either reject the release's own tasks or ignore the rule, which makes the rule untestable in practice.
suggestion: Widen the taxonomy to the kinds the release actually needs - removal, repair, and mechanization (defined as "adds only a check, or the documentation a check reads") - or enumerate the sections that are exempt from the binary.

finding: The §2 repair moved the removal declaration into the task's acceptance ('Every task in this release is one of two kinds, declared in its own acceptance ... whose acceptance names what it removes and what still covers it'), but §2.1 was not updated and still puts the same fact in the closing evidence ('Every removal states, in the closing evidence, what now covers the thing removed'), under a table column headed 'The evidence names'. The same obligation now has two artifacts, and a unit cannot tell whether writing it once in acceptance satisfies §2.1 or whether the pair must be kept in sync.
suggestion: Pick one artifact. Acceptance is the one §2 now relies on and the one a decomposition review can see before implementation: restate §2.1's table as 'The acceptance names', or say explicitly that acceptance declares the kind and evidence records its discharge.

finding: Two mechanics are left to the implementer. (a) init's read-modify-write is a stat at one statement and a write ~30 lines later; §3 says "both read-modify-writes move inside `WithFileLock`" but an implementer reading it as "move the write" leaves the check-then-write window exactly as it is — the stat must move inside the critical section too, and re-run there. (b) The only failure §3 documents is the lock timeout (exit 4). Serialization introduces a second, more likely failure: an import that waits and then re-reads a target another writer just populated now hits the existence guard and exits 3, deterministically, where the racy version exited 0 by overwriting. "The success path gains no flag and no output change" is true and beside the point.
suggestion: Say explicitly that init's existence stat and import's two reads all move inside the lock and are evaluated there, and add one sentence on the serialized loser: an import whose target gained tasks while it waited exits 3 with the existing already-exists message, which is the intended outcome rather than a regression.

finding: §3 asserts "These are the only two remaining unlocked task-file writes; after this section there are none", but §12 has no test for that invariant - only the per-command tests of items 1 and 2. A release that mechanizes the lint-rule table, the flag inventory and the guard set precisely because prose drifts leaves its most load-bearing claim verified by hand once, so a new unlocked write path can join the codebase silently, which is the same failure mode §8.2 describes for the rule table.
suggestion: Add a test in the shape §8.2/§8.3 use: enumerate the sites that write a task file (e.g. every caller of the write helper) and assert each is reached under `WithFileLock`; or, if static enumeration is impractical, require an exemption marker at any unlocked site plus an equality over the marker set, as §4 does with `line-cap:`.

finding: §3 names three entries into the unlocked paths - `importcmd.go`, `init.go`, and `tp add --spec` reaching init "by calling `runInit` before taking its own lock" - but §12 tests only `tp import` and `tp init`. After the change, `add --spec` acquires the write lock twice in sequence, and the spec says neither whether that pair must be atomic (what a concurrent writer may observe between the two acquisitions) nor whether the acquisitions may nest, which is a plausible implementation and a plausible self-deadlock. Nothing in §12 would catch either outcome.
suggestion: State whether `tp add --spec` performs one acquisition spanning init+add or two sequential ones, and what an interleaved writer may observe between them. Add a test: `tp add --spec` on a fresh spec completes within the lock-timeout budget (no self-deadlock) and the resulting file contains both the initialised shell and the added task.

finding: §3 was widened (round 1 idx 5) from one unlocked writer to two — importcmd.go plus init.go, reached by 'tp add --spec' via runInit — but the sections that enumerate this release's defects were not widened with it. §1's table still carries a single row, 'tp import writes the task file outside the write lock'; §2 (also repaired this round) admits a repair task only if it is 'one of the defects in §1 and §9'; and §11 item 1 counts 'the three write defects of §1'. Under the repaired §2 the init.go lock fix is a task of no legal kind, and a unit that resolves the conflict by dropping it ships the path §3 says must not remain ('These are the only two remaining unlocked task-file writes; after this section there are none').
suggestion: Add a second row to §1's table for the init.go / 'tp add --spec' write path and update §11 item 1's enumeration to match, so §2's 'one of the defects in §1 and §9' test admits both repair tasks.

finding: Round 1 idx 28 established that 'contains -race' is an insufficient predicate (a gate edited down to 'go test -race ./...' passes it with golangci-lint gone), and the repair strengthened §12 item 5 to an equality with the exact gate string. §5's own requirement sentence was not updated: it still reads, in bold, 'the gate resolved for every spec/*.tasks.json in this repository contains -race'. The section states the predicate its own test was repaired to reject, and an implementer reading §5 as the requirement builds the weaker assertion.
suggestion: Restate §5's bolded requirement as the equality — the gate resolved for every spec/*.tasks.json is exactly 'go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run' — matching §12 item 5.

finding: Round 1 idx 7 asked how an already-authored, non-settable override is changed. The repair answers with an outcome ('reached by removing the redundant overrides rather than by editing each one') and still names no mechanism. quality_gate is init-authored and read-only at the task level (tp set --workflow rejects it), Non-Goal 3 forbids adding a flag for it, and the unit brief's scope fence forbids hand-editing <base>.tasks.json — so the task that must carry out §5 has no stated legal way to do it, and 'rather than by editing each one' explicitly rules out the obvious illegal one.
suggestion: Name the mechanism the task uses — tp config --extract is the existing candidate for hoisting a value shared by every task file — and state whether removing an init-authored quality_gate sits inside or outside the unit scope fence for this release.

finding: §5 requires the resolved gate for every `spec/*.tasks.json` to contain `-race`, 'reached by removing the redundant overrides rather than by editing each one'. That removal has no sanctioned mechanism under tp's existing contracts, which this spec does not say it changes: `quality_gate` is init-authored and read-only at the task level (`tp set --workflow` does not accept it), Non-Goal 3 forbids adding a command or flag that would, and hand-editing `<base>.tasks.json` is forbidden by this repository's own execution rules. The requirement is stated without naming the operation that satisfies it.
suggestion: State the mechanism explicitly and mark it as operator-sanctioned for this release (e.g. the same thinning migration v0.26.0 performed on the `workflow` blocks, done once as a release migration task with `tp config --resolved` before/after as evidence), or say which existing command performs it.

finding: §6.1 reasons explicitly about what a gate-widening change does to the release: enabling `dupl` and bringing the tree clean must be one task, because otherwise the enabling task's own `tp done` closes red and every later task inherits a red gate. §5 widens the same shared gate with `-race` and carries no equivalent statement: the spec never asserts the tree is race-clean today (it only says the v0.33.0 audit found one race), never makes '`go test -race ./...` is clean' part of the §5 task's acceptance, and never says what happens if `-race` surfaces further races. The failure mode §6.1 names is reachable through §5 by exactly the same path.
suggestion: Mirror §6.1's treatment: state the §5 task's acceptance as '`go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run` is clean', require any race the switch surfaces to be fixed in that same task (the count is discovered, not planned), and note that the gate change and the fixes cannot be split.

finding: §6.1's task acceptance is '`golangci-lint run` is clean with `dupl` enabled', and the escape hatch permits raising the threshold 'to the lowest value at which the tree is clean'. Nothing orders the two operations, so raising the threshold first satisfies the acceptance with zero clones merged and zero duplication removed — the section closes green having done nothing, which contradicts §2's subtraction mandate. Non-Goal 7 is the intended gate on the escape ('would require designing a new abstraction'), but that judgement is per clone and nothing records or checks it.
suggestion: Order the procedure: run at the default threshold, then for each reported clone either merge it or record an exemption at the site with a reason, and raise the threshold only for the clones Non-Goal 7 excludes — with the raise recorded in `.golangci.yml` naming those clones. Then the acceptance cannot be met by the raise alone.

finding: The release's first task 'produces the list as its only output' — guard tests named `file:function` — and §12 item 11 requires a test to compare the marker set against 'the surviving subset of §7.1's list'. The spec never says where that list lives. If it lives only in the task's closing evidence, no test can read it; if the `// guard:` markers themselves are taken as the list, item 11's equality compares the marker set to itself and asserts nothing.
suggestion: Name a durable committed artifact for the list (path and format, e.g. one `file:function` per line), require the first task to write it, and state that item 11's test reads that file as the listed side.

finding: §7.1 makes "The release's first task produce the list as its only output" — a fixed list of guard tests named file:function. Two costs are unpaid. (1) §2 states that every task in this release is either a removal or a repair and "a task that is neither does not belong in this release"; a task whose only output is an inventory is neither, so the release's own first task violates its governing rule. (2) The list has no stated durable home, yet §12 item 11 asserts against "§7.1's list" — so the assertion needs an artifact the spec never names, and each downstream sweep task needs to read it. Left unstated, the task will emit it into closing evidence, where the brief re-injects it into every dependent unit's context: a ~dozens-of-lines inventory paid on every read rather than once.
suggestion: Name the artifact and its home (e.g. a committed file such as spec/0.34.0-guards.txt, one file:function per line), state that the task's evidence points at it rather than reproducing it, and extend §2 with a third kind (a scoping task) or make the list an input the operator produces at decomposition time rather than a task in the release.

finding: The §8.1 repair narrowed README to 'What tp is, install, a one-line-per-command index for discovery' and moved mid-cycle detail into SKILL.md, but §8.2 was not updated and still assigns README the full lint-rule table — 'README.md documents 9 lint rules; the engine emits about 20 ... the table lists every rule the engine can emit, with one line each'. Roughly twenty rule descriptions is not a one-line-per-command index, and the exhaustive-detail row of the repaired table points at the reference instead. §12 item 9 names no document at all, so the ownership gap idx 37 closed for the -race fact is open again for the lint table.
suggestion: State the lint table's home in §8.2 under the repaired economy rule (the reference for exhaustive detail, or SKILL.md if an agent needs it mid-cycle) and name that document in §12 item 9, as §8.3 and item 10 now do.

finding: §5 changes the gate to `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run` and calls `skills/tp/SKILL.md` 'the single home for it under §8.1', but §8.1's table assigns `CLAUDE.md` 'this repository's own conventions', and this repository's gate command is stated in CLAUDE.md (Quick Reference and the per-task rule). Neither §5 nor §8 settles which document owns the repo's own gate string, and §8.1's rule only cuts duplicates from the non-owner — it does not require the owner's copy to be corrected. The doc sweep can therefore ship with CLAUDE.md still stating the pre-`-race` gate, in the release whose §8 exists to stop documents stating false facts.
suggestion: Distinguish the two facts in §8.1: the general `-race` recommendation (SKILL.md) and this repository's own gate command (CLAUDE.md), and state that §5's change updates the CLAUDE.md copy in the same task, so the owner's copy is corrected, not merely de-duplicated.

finding: The repair for idx 39/41 introduces new production surface into a subtraction release: 'The engine gains an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers.' Its only caller is the equality test, which is exactly what §6.2 of the same release removes ('a helper with one call site ... Each is inlined unless a second caller exists today and can be named'), and §2.3 records exported symbols as a before/after count in the direction of fewer. §7.4 protects the §8 equality tests from the test sweep, but nothing protects their production-side source from §6.2, so two tasks in this release are chartered against each other.
suggestion: Extend §7.4's protection to name the §8.2 enumeration (and any other instrument this release adds) as out of scope for §6.2, or state that the enumeration is package-internal and consumed by an in-package test, so it is not new exported surface.

finding: §8.2 keeps the complete rule table in `README.md` ('`README.md` documents 9 lint rules ... the table lists every rule the engine can emit'), but §8.1's ownership table gives README only 'what tp is, install, a one-line-per-command index for discovery' and gives the Reference 'exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail' — an exhaustive one-line-per-rule table is precisely the latter. §8.3, by contrast, now names its documented side explicitly (`skills/tp/SKILL.md`); §8.2 never says which document §12 item 9's equality test reads.
suggestion: Assign the rule table a home under §8.1's own rule (Reference for the exhaustive table, README keeping a pointer, or SKILL.md if an agent needs it mid-cycle — and say which), and name that document as the documented side of item 9, the way §8.3 does.

finding: §8.2 never names which document holds the complete rule table, nor how it is parsed. It opens with "`README.md` documents 9 lint rules" and then says "the table lists every rule the engine can emit", while §8.1 assigns README only "a one-line-per-command index for discovery" and assigns the Reference "exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail", and §8.3's checked inventory is placed in SKILL.md. Three defensible homes means the equality test does not know which file to read; §8.3 names both of its sides, §8.2 names neither.
suggestion: Name the owning document for the lint rule table and reconcile it with §8.1's ownership row, then pin the extraction rule (e.g. rows of the table under a named heading, first column, backticked identifier).

finding: §8.2 says "The engine gains an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers" so the README table can be checked against it. The only consumer named is the equality test. Exporting is a permanent widening of the package's public API to serve an in-repo test that could read an unexported value from the same package — and it is added in the one release that counts exported symbols as a before-and-after subtraction metric (§2.3) and whose Non-Goal 3 says "Every change is a fix, a removal, a hint, a test or a document" (a new exported symbol is none of those five). The surface is paid for forever; the need is satisfied by a same-package test at zero surface cost.
suggestion: Specify an unexported enumeration (e.g. a package-level slice of rule ids) with the equality test living in the same package, and say so explicitly so a task does not export it by reflex. If it must be exported for the test to live elsewhere, name that reason in §8.2 and add the symbol to §11's enumeration and to §2.3's count so the metric is not read as a regression.

finding: The CLI side of the flag equality is pinned ("every flag registered on any command, with a persistent flag counted once at the command that declares it"); the documented side is only "the flag inventory in `skills/tp/SKILL.md`", with no statement of where that inventory begins and ends or how a flag token is recognized in markdown. Membership of flag variants is equally open: negated forms (`--no-compact`, `--no-quiet`, `--no-color`), shorthands, and hidden or deprecated flags are each defensible either way, and each choice flips the test's result today.
suggestion: Pin the documented side the way the CLI side is pinned: a named section or table in SKILL.md, one row per flag, long form in the first column. State explicitly whether negated forms, shorthands and hidden flags are members of the CLI-side set.

finding: The documented side of the equality does not exist and its format is unstated. `skills/tp/SKILL.md` has no flag inventory today — no heading and no per-command flag list — so §8.3 requires authoring one, and §12 item 10 requires a test to extract flags from Markdown prose with no stated shape to key on. The keying is also undecided in a way that matters here: `--stdin` is registered on `add` as well as on `done`/`close`, so a name-keyed inventory reports `--stdin` as documented (README documents `tp add --stdin`) while `done --stdin` stays undocumented — the defect §8.3 opens with.
suggestion: Fix the extraction contract: name the SKILL.md heading that holds the inventory, state that each entry is a `<command> --<flag>` pair in a backticked span (persistent flags listed once under the declaring command), and say that the test reads only that section — so README's command index cannot satisfy the equality.

finding: The repair for idx 42/43 settles one of the four boundary questions round 1 raised (persistent flags counted once at the declaring command) and states the rule as though it were complete: 'the CLI side is every flag registered on any command'. Cobra registers --help on every command and --version on root, and the spec is still silent on shorthands, on hidden or deprecated flags, and on the negated forms --no-compact / --no-color / --no-quiet that round 1 named explicitly. Read literally, the new wording requires SKILL.md's inventory to carry --help once per command or the equality test fails; read loosely it is the same undefined set as before, now with an authoritative-sounding sentence over it.
suggestion: Close the remaining cases in one clause: auto-generated flags (--help, --version) are excluded, a shorthand is not a separate entry, and each negated form is either a distinct entry or documented on the line of the flag it negates.

finding: Item 6's trailing clause "existing exit codes are unchanged" names no set, so no one can write it as a test or watch it fail: the exit-code surface spans every command and every error path. It reads as reassurance inside a numbered list whose other entries are all executable.
suggestion: Delete the clause - Non-Goal 1 already holds that fence - or bound it to something runnable, e.g. "the exit codes asserted by the existing exit-code tests are unchanged".

finding: "The `line-cap:` markers come out with the exemption" is unqualified, and the tree holds four such markers, not two: `internal/cli/add.go:99` and `internal/cli/set.go:191` (the bulk readers, which do come out) plus `internal/cli/audit.go:715` (git diff output) and `internal/cli/lint.go:147` (spec markdown), which are genuinely non-NDJSON scanners the guard exempts for a different reason. TestNDJSONReadersShareTheCap checks the marker per site rather than against a list, so deleting all four turns the gate red at two sites this section never mentions.
suggestion: Scope the sentence: "the `line-cap:` markers at the two bulk call sites come out; the markers on the non-NDJSON scanners in `audit.go` and `lint.go` stay, since they state a different exception."

finding: In the Non-Goal 7 fallback, §6.1 requires the dupl threshold be raised "to the lowest value at which the tree is clean". Finding a minimum is a search: each probe is a full golangci-lint run over the tree, so pinning the exact minimum costs several gate-length runs to settle a number whose discriminating power is identical to any value just above the largest surviving clone. The sentence was added to replace round 1's unmeasurable "small enough to act on", but it swapped an unmeasurable rule for an expensive one where a satisficing rule costs a single run.
suggestion: Require a recorded threshold above the largest surviving clone and a recorded reason — e.g. "raised to the smallest value the author verified clean in one run, with the clone it accommodates named in the comment" — instead of the true minimum. The audit checks the recorded reason, not the optimality of the number.

finding: The Reference row is the only one of four that names no path. The file is `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md` — it ships inside the skill directory beside SKILL.md, which is precisely why its boundary with SKILL.md is the one boundary the "cut from the non-owner" rule most needs pinned: the table calls it "loaded on demand" while it travels with the always-loaded document. §8.3 names `skills/tp/SKILL.md` exactly, so the asymmetry is visible in the same section.
suggestion: Write the row as `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md` and add one sentence on the SKILL.md/REFERENCE.md split (exhaustive field and schema detail in REFERENCE, the forms an agent uses mid-cycle in SKILL), since a fact duplicated between those two is the case an implementer will hit first.
